acceptance_criteria.statement: Given one model and three proposed uses, the reader assigns tiers and decides each use.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A property portal's valuation model has a median error of about 7% for off-market homes. Three proposals arrive: a badge comparing each asking price with the estimate, a guaranteed purchase offer at 94% of the estimate funded by a partner, and a bank licensing estimates for mortgage pre-approval. Using only this chapter: how do you classify and decide each, and what does the platform need before the badge ships?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Classify by decision: the badge informs, the offer and the mortgage input commit money. The badge ships under rules: shown only when the prediction interval is narrow enough and comparables suffice, thresholds from the interval, an explanation, training labels from recorded sale prices only (never badged asking prices), excluded data enforced in the pipeline, monitoring by segment, named owners, and a district-randomized experiment. The guaranteed offer is declined until back-tested on resale over a holding period and on accepting owners, with a capital limit; the mortgage input needs commit-tier validation and sign-off independent of the builders. Before any of it, the model is registered with an owner, tier, label definition, monitor and cost.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which models matter and what platform runs them; governance by decision tier; features, labels and prediction logs as the hard parts; informing versus committing, with Zillow Offers as the documented case. Then 146 models and one price badge at Veldmark, concepts, platform architecture, the documented record, Valuo and the pricing hint, shared versus per-brand models, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: OLX and Adevinta engineering sources, Zillow filings and shareholder letters, Uber engineering, the EU AI Act, model-card research, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Which ML capabilities matter in listing marketplaces, and what platform runs them responsibly?
thesis.claim: The ML capabilities that matter in a listing marketplace are the ones that make its decisions about listings, buyers and money (category and attribute prediction, image classification, fraud scoring, ranking and recommendations, price estimates and valuations, lead scoring), so a marketplace should classify each production model by the decision it makes (informs, orders, gates or commits), not by its algorithm, and let that tier set the depth of validation, monitoring and approval; run every model on one shared path whose first services are point-in-time-correct features, labels taken from moderation decisions, contacts and sales, and a prediction log joined to outcomes; make registration with an owner, a tier per consumer, a label definition, a monitor and a cost a condition of production access; and move a model to a higher tier only with a new validation regime, new owners and a limit on the money it can commit, because an estimate accurate enough to inform a buyer is not accurate enough to commit money.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that model governance should scale with the model's sophistication, that each brand's data-science team chooses its own training stack and monitoring, and that a model validated for one use can be reused for a more consequential one once it scores well offline.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this owns the inventory and the tier rules rather than the models; withdraws production credentials from unregistered models after a deadline; turns tiers into gates (segment evaluation for inform, two-sided experiments for order, sampled labels, appeals and statements of reasons for gate, independent validation and capital limits for commit); makes label events part of the producing teams' contracts; funds the platform as a product measured by adoption; and treats any promotion to commit as a board-level decision.
thesis.how_why: Veldmark's first inventory in September 2027 found 146 production models on four training stacks, 23 without an owner, 41 without monitoring beyond uptime and 12 that could not be retrained. Valuo, the same model behind three requests, has a median absolute error of 7.4% off-market and 2.3% for listed homes; the badge shipped under eight rules (shown only when the interval width is at most 12% of the midpoint with at least eight comparable sales, DVF prices as the only labels, Keybridge data rejected by a lineage tag), while Hearthly Direct's guaranteed offer at 94% of the estimate was declined because Valuo had never been back-tested on resale or on owners who would accept. Zillow's 2021 wind-down of Zillow Offers is the documented case of an estimate used to commit. Registration became a condition of production access on 9 November 2027.

supporting_claims.claim: The ML capabilities that matter in a listing marketplace are the models that make its decisions about listings, buyers and money, and in most groups they have accumulated team by team into a portfolio nobody can list, own or reproduce.

Governance follows the decision a model makes (inform, order, gate or commit), not its algorithm, and because one model can serve several consumers at different tiers, the tier is assigned per consumer and every consumer must be declared.

The listing-specific hard parts of an ML platform are point-in-time-correct features, labels from moderation decisions, contacts and sales, and a prediction log joined to outcomes; most listing models are scored on events and stored on the listing, and an online feature store pays only for real-time behavioral features.

An estimate accurate enough to inform is not accurate enough to commit money: moving a model to the commit tier needs a new validation regime (forward back-tests on the population that accepts), new owners and a limit on the money it can commit, as the Zillow Offers record and Veldmark's two declined Valuo uses show.

For a consumer-facing estimate, the validation the inform tier sets takes the form of written display, label and data-exclusion rules, with labels taken from recorded sales and the label and exclusion rules enforced by the pipeline rather than by policy, and the estimate is launched as an experiment randomized by area.

Every model runs on one shared path in the sense that it registers in one registry and logs and is monitored to one standard, with registration (owner, tier per consumer, label definition, monitor and cost) a condition of production access; training and serving migrate to the golden path when it is better, so the platform is adopted rather than forced, and model weights are shared only where the task is generic.

role.contribution: Governs the models that now make most of the changes the platform measures, by the consequence of their errors.

sections.heading: Architecture: What an ML Platform for Listings Contains
sections.controlling_idea: An ML platform for listings has seven parts, and the listing-specific design lies in event-triggered scoring stored on the listing, a conditional feature store, labels from proxies with known biases, and monitors for four listing-specific drift sources.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies the platform and its hard parts.

flow.rationale: The seven parts come first so each subsection can name its part; serving comes next because it decides whether features must be online; the feature store follows because it depends on that answer; labels follow features because a model needs both; monitoring comes last because it watches features, labels and predictions together. Reversed, the feature-store rule would come before the reader knows most models are scored on events.

transition_in.introduces: The platform that runs them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The platform has seven parts (data access, training orchestration, model registry, serving, features, labels, and the prediction log with monitoring), and the last three are where listing marketplaces need specific design.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the listing-specific parts are label pipelines, shared feature definitions and the prediction log.
evidence.shows: Shows where listing design concentrates.

advances_thesis.how: Names the components and marks the listing-specific ones.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because a listing changes rarely compared with how often it is viewed, batch or event-triggered scoring with the result stored on the listing is the default serving mode for most listing-level models.

evidence.what: A Tradeyard listing published once, edited a few times and viewed hundreds of times; rescoring on ListingUpdated.
evidence.shows: Shows why scoring on change beats scoring on view.

evidence.what: Serving modes: batch, event-triggered asynchronous, synchronous endpoint, in-engine scoring; when each fits, examples and main risk.
evidence.shows: Shows that only request-time inputs need synchronous serving.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the default serving mode.

transition_in.carries_over: Serving as one of the seven parts.
transition_in.introduces: Which serving mode most listing models need.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Zillow's 2020 floor-plan detection shows the event-triggered mode in practice: inference attached to the media lifecycle as batch jobs, chosen because a live endpoint took far longer to create.

evidence.what: Zillow Tech Hub 2020: panoramas land in storage, a workflow launches batch-transform jobs for window and door detection; endpoint about ten minutes to create versus a one-to-two-minute batch start (current state not public).
evidence.shows: Shows the pattern chosen for cost and simplicity.

advances_thesis.how: Documents the default serving mode.

transition_in.introduces: A documented case of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In-engine scoring is the documented pattern for ranking, and the platform's job there is to keep the model's features fresh in the index and its version in the registry.

evidence.what: OLX Tech 2022: LambdaMART trained with XGBoost, run inside Solr's learning-to-rank plugin, some features 'refreshed periodically (e.g. CTR)' (current setup may differ).
evidence.shows: Shows the model living in the engine.

advances_thesis.how: Documents the in-engine mode and the platform's role in it.

transition_in.introduces: The in-engine mode for ranking.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Feature stores are the most oversold part of ML platforms in this industry: no classifieds company has documented one, and the documented platforms work without one or with stores under another name.

evidence.what: Adevinta Tech Blog 2024 (Kubeflow, MLflow, no feature store); OLX Tech 2025 (ScyllaDB and DynamoDB as an online store without the name).
evidence.shows: Shows the public record of classifieds platforms without a feature store.

advances_thesis.how: Challenges the default assumption that a platform starts with a feature store.

transition_in.carries_over: Serving modes that read scores stored on the listing.
transition_in.introduces: The feature store, usually assumed necessary.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Many listing models need no feature store because their features are intrinsic to the listing, and a store pays only for aggregated behavioral features shared by several models and, almost always, for real-time behavioral features.

evidence.what: Feature kinds: listing-intrinsic, aggregated behavioral (batch), real-time behavioral (streaming); where each lives without a store and when a store pays.
evidence.shows: Shows that the need depends on the kind of feature.

advances_thesis.how: Says when a feature store is worth its cost.

transition_in.carries_over: No classifieds feature store is documented.
transition_in.introduces: Why many listing models do not need one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rule is to build or buy an online feature store when real-time behavioral features drive a gate-tier or order-tier model, and until then to standardize feature definitions in the lakehouse and log features at prediction time, which solves training-serving skew.

evidence.what: Airbnb's Chronon README: features defined once, point-in-time-correct backfills, consistency job comparing backfills with logged fetches.
evidence.shows: Shows the full version of the idea that logged features approximate.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the decision rule for the feature store.

transition_in.introduces: The rule that follows from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A classifieds marketplace usually never sees the sale, so its labels come from proxies (contacts, delisting, moderator decisions, registered transaction prices), each with its own bias.

evidence.what: OLX Tech 2022: ranking trained on purchases 'or messages/calls to sellers' because 'transactions aren't always confirmed'.
evidence.shows: Shows contacts used as labels and why.

evidence.what: Delisting after contact as a sale proxy; the 'mark as sold' button; moderators blind to what they did not see; DVF lagging the market by months.
evidence.shows: Shows the bias of each proxy.

advances_thesis.how: Names the label proxies and their biases.

transition_in.carries_over: Features, the inputs a model needs.
transition_in.introduces: Labels, the outcomes it learns from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The label pipeline is a product with an owner, a definition and a delay, because choosing the label is choosing what the marketplace optimizes, which is the mechanism behind Vanity Liquidity.

evidence.what: A ranking model trained on clicks learns to produce clicks.
evidence.shows: Shows the label deciding the objective.

advances_thesis.how: Makes labels an owned contract.

transition_in.carries_over: Every label is a biased proxy.
transition_in.introduces: Why the label pipeline needs an owner and a contract.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Beyond generic drift, listing marketplaces have four drift sources that need explicit monitors: taxonomy and schema changes, seasonality and market shifts, adversarial drift and feedback loops.

evidence.what: Tradeyard's bikes split on Monday 1 November 2027 gives every category-using model a new value.
evidence.shows: Shows taxonomy change as drift.

evidence.what: Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015: 'hidden feedback loops' and 'undeclared consumers'.
evidence.shows: Names the feedback-loop and consumer problems from research.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies what the monitoring part must watch.

transition_in.carries_over: Labels, the last input to training.
transition_in.introduces: Monitoring what changes after deployment.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark chooses a hybrid platform, registry and monitoring first and migration later, builds what differentiates and buys commodity models, and controls cost through architecture.

advances_thesis.how: Weighs platform strategies, build or buy, and cost.

transition_in.introduces: The platform strategy that sharing runs on, and its costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Of the platform strategies, Veldmark chooses the hybrid under the decision of 9 November 2027, under which the Valuo badge launched: one mandatory registry and monitoring standard over heterogeneous training and serving, because registration first and migration later avoids The Forced Fit; for individual capabilities a different rule applies: build where they differentiate, buy where they are commodity.

evidence.what: Platform strategy table: managed suite per brand, one suite group-wide, open-source golden path, hybrid.
evidence.shows: Shows why the hybrid fits groups after acquisitions.

evidence.what: Decision of Tuesday 9 November 2027: MLflow registry and prediction-log standard mandatory; AWS golden path for Tradeyard and Motorvane; Hearthly keeps Vertex AI, Keybridge Azure ML.

evidence.shows: Shows build-or-buy decided by differentiation.

conclusion.heading: From Models to Many Markets
conclusion.synthesis: The tier says who bears an error, the platform's labels, prediction log and registry are what let anyone measure that error for each consumer, and promotion to a higher tier is allowed only when that measurement exists for the new use; Valuo shows all three in one model.
conclusion.so_what: The expensive errors sit in the uses nobody classified: a group that cannot list its models cannot tell which of them already commit money.

takeaway.content: Register every model with an owner, a tier per consumer, a label, a monitor and a cost, and promote none to commit without a new validation regime and a limit.
